facts.fact: A.O. Hume, a retired British civil servant, organised the founding of the Congress in December 1885.
Dadabhai Naoroji propounded the Drain of Wealth theory.
Tilak's slogan was 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it'.
Swadeshi and Boycott were first adopted in the agitation against the Partition of Bengal (1905).
The Home Rule Leagues of 1916 were led by Tilak and Annie Besant.
Non-Cooperation was withdrawn after the Chauri Chaura incident (1922).
The Swaraj Party was formed by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru.
The Purna Swaraj resolution was adopted at the Lahore session (1929).
Quit India was launched with the slogan 'Do or Die'.
The Ghadar Party had its headquarters at San Francisco.
The Simon Commission was boycotted because it had no Indian member.
Chronology: Second RTC (1931) → Quit India (1942) → RIN Mutiny (1946).
Alluri Sitarama Raju led the Rampa Rebellion (1922–24).
The Bangabhasha Prakasika Sabha (1836) was formed by associates of Raja Rammohan Roy.
The Landholders' Society (1837, Calcutta) was founded by Dwarkanath Tagore to protect zamindars' interests.
The Bengal British India Society (1843) was formed by William Adam.
The British Indian Association (1851, Calcutta) had Radhakant Deb as president and Debendranath Tagore as secretary.
The Madras Native Association (1852) was founded by Gajula Lakshminarasu Chetty.
The Bombay Association (1852) was founded by Jagannath Shankarsheth.
The London Indian Society (1865) was founded by Dadabhai Naoroji with W.C. Bonnerjee and others.
The East India Association (1866, London) was founded by Dadabhai Naoroji to present Indian views to the British public.
The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870) was founded by M.G. Ranade, G.V. Joshi and others.
The National Indian Association (1870) was founded by Mary Carpenter for female education.
The Indian League (1875) was founded by Sisir Kumar Ghosh.
The Indian (National) Association (1876, Calcutta) was founded by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose.
The Indian National Conference (1883) of Surendranath Banerjee merged with the Congress in 1886.
The Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884) was founded by M. Veeraraghavachariar, G. Subramania Iyer and P. Ananda Charlu.
The Bombay Presidency Association (1885) was founded by Pherozeshah Mehta, K.T. Telang and Badruddin Tyabji.
A.O. Hume first formed the Indian National Union (1884), renamed the Indian National Congress in 1885 on Dadabhai Naoroji's suggestion.
The Vernacular Press Act (1878) of Lord Lytton — the "Gagging Act" — curbed Indian-language papers; Ripon repealed it in 1882.
The Arms Act (1878) of Lytton made it an offence for Indians to carry arms without a licence.
Under Lytton (1876) the maximum age for the ICS examination was cut from 21 to 19, hurting Indian candidates.
The 1877 Delhi Durbar proclaimed Victoria Empress of India (Kaisar-i-Hind) in the middle of a famine.
The Ilbert Bill (1883, Ripon) let Indian judges try Europeans; the 'white mutiny' forced a compromise (jury half European).
Lord Dufferin was Viceroy when the Congress was founded and later called it a "microscopic minority" (1888).
The "safety valve" theory was put forward by Lala Lajpat Rai (Young India, 1916), drawing on Wedderburn's biography of Hume.
Historians (Bipan Chandra) argue the founders used Hume as a "lightning conductor" to avoid official hostility.
The first session opened on 28 December 1885 at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay.
The first session was planned for Poona but shifted to Bombay because of cholera.
Delegates rose from 72 at Bombay (1885) to 434 at Calcutta (1886).
The 1886 Calcutta session decided to set up Provincial Congress Committees.
In 1890 Kadambini Ganguly, one of the first women graduates, addressed the Congress.
Bonnerjee's stated aims were friendship among Indians of all regions, removal of race-creed-region prejudice and national unity.
The 1885 Congress session met at Bombay under W.C. Bonnerjee.
The 1886 Congress session met at Calcutta under Dadabhai Naoroji.
The 1887 Congress session met at Madras under Badruddin Tyabji.
The 1888 Congress session met at Allahabad under George Yule.
The 1889 Congress session met at Bombay under William Wedderburn.
The 1890 Congress session met at Calcutta under Pherozeshah Mehta.
The 1891 Congress session met at Nagpur under P. Ananda Charlu.
The 1892 Congress session met at Allahabad under W.C. Bonnerjee.
The 1893 Congress session met at Lahore under Dadabhai Naoroji.
The 1894 Congress session met at Madras under Alfred Webb.
The 1895 Congress session met at Poona under Surendranath Banerjee.
The 1896 Congress session met at Calcutta under Rahimtulla M. Sayani.
The 1897 Congress session met at Amraoti under C. Sankaran Nair.
The 1898 Congress session met at Madras under Ananda Mohan Bose.
The 1899 Congress session met at Lucknow under Romesh Chunder Dutt.
The 1900 Congress session met at Lahore under N.G. Chandavarkar.
The 1901 Congress session met at Calcutta under Dinshaw E. Wacha.
The 1902 Congress session met at Ahmedabad under Surendranath Banerjee.
The 1903 Congress session met at Madras under Lal Mohan Ghosh.
The 1904 Congress session met at Bombay under Henry Cotton.
The 1905 Congress session met at Benares under Gopal Krishna Gokhale.
The 1906 Congress session met at Calcutta under Dadabhai Naoroji.
The 1907 Congress session met at Surat under Rash Behari Ghosh.
The 1908 Congress session met at Madras under Rash Behari Ghosh.
The 1909 Congress session met at Lahore under Madan Mohan Malaviya.
The 1910 Congress session met at Allahabad under William Wedderburn.
The 1911 Congress session met at Calcutta under Bishan Narayan Dar.
The 1912 Congress session met at Bankipore (Patna) under R.N. Mudholkar.
The 1913 Congress session met at Karachi under Nawab Syed Mohammad Bahadur.
The 1914 Congress session met at Madras under Bhupendra Nath Bose.
The 1915 Congress session met at Bombay under S.P. Sinha.
The 1916 Congress session met at Lucknow under Ambica Charan Mazumdar.
The 1917 Congress session met at Calcutta under Annie Besant.
The 1918 (Special) Congress session met at Bombay (Special, Aug) under Syed Hasan Imam.
The 1918 Congress session met at Delhi under Madan Mohan Malaviya.
The 1919 Congress session met at Amritsar under Motilal Nehru.
The 1920 (Special) Congress session met at Calcutta (Special, Sept) under Lala Lajpat Rai.
The 1920 Congress session met at Nagpur under C. Vijayaraghavachariar.
The 1921 Congress session met at Ahmedabad under Hakim Ajmal Khan (for C.R. Das).
The 1922 Congress session met at Gaya under C.R. Das.
The 1923 (Special) Congress session met at Delhi (Special, Sept) under Abul Kalam Azad.
The 1923 (Dec) Congress session met at Kakinada (Cocanada) under Maulana Mohammad Ali.
The 1924 Congress session met at Belgaum under M.K. Gandhi.
The 1925 Congress session met at Kanpur (Cawnpore) under Sarojini Naidu.
The 1926 Congress session met at Gauhati under S. Srinivasa Iyengar.
The 1927 Congress session met at Madras under M.A. Ansari.
The 1928 Congress session met at Calcutta under Motilal Nehru.
The 1929 Congress session met at Lahore under Jawaharlal Nehru.
The 1931 Congress session met at Karachi under Vallabhbhai Patel.
The 1932 Congress session met at Delhi under Amrit Ranchhoddas Seth.
The 1933 Congress session met at Calcutta under Nellie Sengupta.
The 1934 Congress session met at Bombay under Rajendra Prasad.
The 1936 (April) Congress session met at Lucknow under Jawaharlal Nehru.
The 1936 (Dec) Congress session met at Faizpur under Jawaharlal Nehru.
The 1938 Congress session met at Haripura under Subhas Chandra Bose.
The 1939 Congress session met at Tripuri under Subhas Chandra Bose.
The 1940 Congress session met at Ramgarh under Abul Kalam Azad.
The 1946 Congress session met at Meerut under J.B. Kripalani.
The 1948 Congress session met at Jaipur under Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
At the Calcutta session of 1896 Vande Mataram was sung for the first time, by Rabindranath Tagore.
The Lucknow session (1899) demanded an end to the drain of wealth and a permanent fixing of land revenue.
Gandhi first appeared on the Congress platform at the Calcutta session of 1901.
The Calcutta session of 1906 adopted four resolutions — Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott and National Education.
The Congress adopted its first written constitution at Madras in 1908, drafted at the Allahabad Convention.
The Lahore session of 1909 disapproved of separate electorates under the Morley–Minto reforms.
Jana Gana Mana was first sung at the Calcutta session of 1911.
Nagpur (1920) changed the goal to Swaraj by peaceful and legitimate means, set up a 15-member Working Committee and linguistic PCCs, and fixed a four-anna fee.
At Ahmedabad (1921) Maulana Hasrat Mohani moved the first demand for complete independence.
At Gaya (1922) the council-entry proposal of C.R. Das was defeated, so he formed the Swaraj Party.
The Hindustani Seva Dal, the Congress volunteer wing, was founded by N.S. Hardikar at the Kakinada session (1923).
The Madras session (1927) passed a resolution for complete national independence and resolved to boycott the Simon Commission.
The Calcutta session (1928) gave the British a year — Dominion Status by 31 December 1929 or civil disobedience — and saw the All India Youth Congress formed.
Karachi (1931) adopted the resolution on Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme and endorsed the Gandhi–Irwin Pact.
The Bombay session (1934) amended the constitution and made khadi compulsory for elected members.
At Lucknow (April 1936) Nehru urged the Congress to adopt socialism as its goal.
Faizpur (December 1936) was the first Congress session held in a village.
The Haripura session (1938) under Bose led to the National Planning Committee, chaired by Nehru.
After Tripuri (1939) Bose resigned and Rajendra Prasad became president.
Meerut (1946) under Kripalani was the last session before independence and accepted the Cabinet Mission plan.
Dadabhai Naoroji presided over the Congress three times — 1886, 1893 and 1906.
Abul Kalam Azad (1923, aged 35) was the youngest Congress president.
George Yule (1888) was the first English (non-Indian) president of the Congress.
Nellie Sengupta (1933) was the third woman, and an Englishwoman by birth, to preside over the Congress.
No annual sessions were held in 1930, 1935 and 1941–45 (bans, jail and war).
Dadabhai Naoroji, the "Grand Old Man of India", was the first Indian elected to the British House of Commons (1892, Finsbury Central).
Naoroji's drain theory is set out in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901).
R.C. Dutt wrote The Economic History of India, a key economic critique of British rule.
Gopal Krishna Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in 1905 and was Gandhi's political guru.
M.G. Ranade was the political guru of Gokhale.
Surendranath Banerjee edited The Bengalee and was called "Rashtraguru"; he had been dismissed from the ICS.
Pherozeshah Mehta shaped the Bombay Municipal Corporation and founded the Bombay Chronicle (1913).
Dinshaw Wacha was a Moderate concerned with currency and public finance.
The Indian Councils Act 1892 enlarged the councils, brought in indirect election and let members discuss the budget (no vote).
Critics called the Moderates' petitioning 'political mendicancy' and their methods the '3 Ps' — prayer, petition, protest.
Moderate demands included simultaneous ICS examinations in India, separation of executive from judiciary and cuts in military spending.
The Moderates drew support mainly from the educated urban middle class.
The Partition of Bengal was announced on 19–20 July 1905 and took effect on 16 October 1905.
Bengal was split into Eastern Bengal and Assam (capital Dacca) and the rest of Bengal (capital Calcutta).
The Swadeshi (boycott) resolution was passed at the Calcutta Town Hall meeting on 7 August 1905.
16 October 1905 was observed as a day of mourning; people tied rakhis (Raksha Bandhan) and sang Amar Sonar Bangla.
The partition was annulled at the Delhi Durbar of George V on 12 December 1911, when the capital was moved to Delhi.
The National Council of Education was set up on 15 August 1906; Aurobindo Ghosh was principal of its Bengal National College.
V.O. Chidambaram Pillai launched the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company at Tuticorin (1906).
P.C. Ray founded Bengal Chemicals, a Swadeshi enterprise.
Ashwini Kumar Dutta organised the Swadesh Bandhab Samiti at Barisal.
Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata during the Swadeshi years.
Swadeshi spread beyond Bengal — Tilak in Maharashtra, Lajpat Rai and Ajit Singh in Punjab, Syed Haider Raza in Delhi, Chidambaram Pillai in Madras.
Samitis (volunteer bodies) such as Swadesh Bandhab, Brati, Dacca Anushilan and Suhrid became the movement's backbone.
Swadeshi failed to win most Muslim peasants of East Bengal and declined by 1908 under repression and the Surat split.
Tilak ran Kesari (Marathi) and Mahratta (English).
Tilak popularised the Ganapati festival (1893) and the Shivaji festival (1895).
Valentine Chirol called Tilak the 'Father of Indian Unrest'.
Tilak was jailed at Mandalay (1908–14), where he wrote Gita Rahasya.
Tilak was first jailed for sedition in 1897 after the Poona plague-measures agitation.
Lala Lajpat Rai was called 'Punjab Kesari'; he was deported to Mandalay with Ajit Singh in 1907.
Lajpat Rai founded the Indian Home Rule League of America (New York, 1917) and wrote Unhappy India and Young India.
Lajpat Rai founded the Servants of the People Society (1921).
Bipin Chandra Pal was called the 'Father of Revolutionary Thoughts'; he edited New India and Paridarshak.
Aurobindo Ghosh edited the English daily Bande Mataram and outlined passive resistance; after the Alipore case he left for Pondicherry (1910).
Lal–Bal–Pal = Lala Lajpat Rai (Punjab), Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Maharashtra), Bipin Chandra Pal (Bengal).
Japan's defeat of Russia (1905) and Moderate failures fed the rise of the Extremists.
Curzon also passed the Calcutta Corporation Act (1899), the Official Secrets Act (1904) and the Indian Universities Act (1904).
A Muslim deputation led by the Aga Khan met Viceroy Minto at Simla on 1 October 1906 to ask for separate electorates.
The All-India Muslim League was founded at Dacca on 30 December 1906 under Nawab Salimullah; the Aga Khan was its first president.
Jinnah joined the Muslim League in 1913 while remaining in the Congress.
The Indian Councils Act 1909 (Morley–Minto) introduced separate electorates for Muslims; Minto is called the "father of communal electorate".
Under the 1909 Act S.P. Sinha became the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council (Law Member).
John Morley was Secretary of State and Lord Minto the Viceroy behind the 1909 reforms.
The 1909 Act raised the Imperial Legislative Council from 16 to 60 additional members and let members move resolutions.
At Surat (1907) the Moderates wanted to drop the 1906 resolutions and the Extremists wanted Lajpat Rai or Tilak as president.
After Surat the Moderates held the Allahabad Convention (April 1908) and wrote a constitution that kept the Extremists out.
The government struck with the Seditious Meetings Act (1907), the Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act (1908) and the Indian Press Act (1910).
Tilak's Home Rule League began in April 1916 at Belgaum and covered Maharashtra (except Bombay city), Karnataka, Central Provinces and Berar.
Annie Besant's Home Rule League began in September 1916 at Madras (Adyar) and covered the rest of India.
Annie Besant ran the papers New India and Commonweal.
The Home Rule idea was borrowed from the Irish Home Rule movement.
Besant was interned in June 1917; protests won her release and the presidency of the 1917 Calcutta session.
Montagu's August Declaration (20 August 1917) promised 'responsible government' by stages.
Home Rule drew in Jinnah, Motilal Nehru, Jawaharlal Nehru, Tej Bahadur Sapru and others; its network later served Gandhi.
In the Lucknow Pact (December 1916) the Congress accepted separate electorates and the League joined in demanding self-government; Tilak and Jinnah were its architects.
The Lucknow session of 1916 also readmitted the Extremists into the Congress.
The Chapekar brothers shot the plague commissioner W.C. Rand at Poona in 1897 — the first political murder of the period.
V.D. Savarkar founded the Mitra Mela (1899), which became the Abhinav Bharat Society (1904).
The Anushilan Samiti was founded at Calcutta (1902) by Pramatha Mitra; its Dacca branch was led by Pulin Behari Das.
Barindra Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendranath Dutta brought out the revolutionary weekly Yugantar (1906); the Jugantar group grew from it.
On 30 April 1908 Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki threw a bomb at Muzaffarpur meant for judge Kingsford.
Khudiram Bose was hanged in August 1908, aged about 18; Prafulla Chaki shot himself.
The Alipore (Manicktolla) Bomb Case (1908–09) tried Aurobindo and Barindra Ghosh; C.R. Das won Aurobindo's acquittal.
Madan Lal Dhingra assassinated Curzon Wyllie in London in July 1909.
Anant Kanhere shot Nasik collector A.M.T. Jackson in 1909 (Nasik Conspiracy Case); Savarkar was transported to the Andamans.
Shyamji Krishna Varma founded India House in London (1905) and the journal Indian Sociologist.
Madame Bhikaji Cama unfurled an Indian flag at the International Socialist Congress, Stuttgart (1907), and ran Bande Mataram from Paris.
Virendranath Chattopadhyay published Talwar from Berlin and led the Berlin Committee (1915).
In the Delhi Conspiracy Case a bomb was thrown at Viceroy Hardinge in Delhi (23 December 1912); Rash Behari Bose planned it.
Jatin Mukherjee ("Bagha Jatin") died fighting the police at Balasore (1915) during the German-arms plot.
The Ghadar Party was founded in 1913 with headquarters at San Francisco (Yugantar Ashram); Sohan Singh Bhakna was president and Lala Har Dayal its moving spirit.
The party's weekly Ghadar first appeared on 1 November 1913.
Kartar Singh Sarabha, a young Ghadarite, was hanged in 1915 in the Lahore Conspiracy Case.
The Komagata Maru (1914), chartered by Gurdit Singh, was turned away from Vancouver; on return its passengers were fired on at Budge Budge.
The Ghadarites planned a rising for 21 February 1915; it was betrayed, and only the Singapore garrison mutinied (15 February 1915).
A Provisional Government of India was set up at Kabul (1915) with Raja Mahendra Pratap as president and Barkatullah as prime minister.
The Hindustan Republican Association (HRA) was founded at Kanpur in October 1924 by Sachindranath Sanyal, Ramprasad Bismil and others.
The HRA robbed a train at Kakori near Lucknow on 9 August 1925.
Ramprasad Bismil, Ashfaqullah Khan, Rajendra Lahiri and Roshan Singh were hanged for Kakori (1927).
Ramprasad Bismil is linked with the song 'Sarfaroshi ki Tamanna'.
The HRA became the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) at Feroz Shah Kotla, Delhi, in September 1928 under Chandrashekhar Azad.
Bhagat Singh founded the Naujawan Bharat Sabha at Lahore (1926).
To avenge Lajpat Rai, Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Azad shot ASP J.P. Saunders at Lahore on 17 December 1928.
Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly on 8 April 1929 against the Public Safety and Trade Disputes Bills.
Jatin Das died in Lahore jail on 13 September 1929, on the 64th day of his hunger strike.
Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru were hanged at Lahore on 23 March 1931 (Lahore Conspiracy Case); the day is Shaheed Diwas.
Chandrashekhar Azad died in an encounter at Alfred Park, Allahabad, on 27 February 1931.
Bhagat Singh wrote 'Why I Am an Atheist' in jail.
Surya Sen ("Masterda") led the Chittagong Armoury Raid on 18 April 1930 in the name of the Indian Republican Army.
Pritilata Waddedar (died 1932) and Kalpana Dutt were women fighters of the Chittagong group.
Surya Sen was hanged in January 1934.
Benoy, Badal and Dinesh attacked the Writers' Building, Calcutta, in December 1930 and shot Inspector-General Simpson.
Bina Das fired at Bengal Governor Stanley Jackson at the Calcutta University convocation (1932).
Udham Singh shot Michael O'Dwyer, Punjab's Lt-Governor at the time of Jallianwala, in London on 13 March 1940.
The Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929) tried communist and trade-union leaders.
The Montagu–Chelmsford Report (1918) led to the Government of India Act 1919.
The 1919 Act introduced dyarchy in the provinces — "reserved" subjects under the governor and "transferred" subjects under Indian ministers.
The 1919 Act made the central legislature bicameral (Council of State and Legislative Assembly) and introduced direct elections.
The 1919 Act extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians and Europeans.
The 1919 Act created a High Commissioner for India in London and provided for a Public Service Commission (set up 1926).
The Rowlatt Act (March 1919), officially the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act, followed the Sedition Committee of Justice Sidney Rowlatt.
The Rowlatt Act allowed detention without trial — summed up as 'no vakil, no daleel, no appeal'.
Gandhi called an all-India hartal against the Rowlatt Act on 6 April 1919 through his Satyagraha Sabha.
The arrest of Saifuddin Kitchlew and Satyapal at Amritsar led to the Jallianwala Bagh meeting.
On 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi) General Reginald Dyer fired on a crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar; O'Dwyer was the Lt-Governor.
The government appointed the Hunter Committee (Disorders Inquiry Committee) in October 1919.
Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood in protest; Gandhi returned his Kaiser-i-Hind medal (1920).
The Khilafat Committee (1919) was led by the Ali brothers (Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali), Maulana Azad, Hakim Ajmal Khan and Hasrat Mohani.
Khilafat Day was observed on 17 October 1919; Gandhi presided over the All-India Khilafat Conference at Delhi in November 1919.
Non-Cooperation formally began on 1 August 1920 — the day Tilak died.
The Tilak Swaraj Fund aimed at ₹1 crore; the Bezawada AICC (1921) set targets of one crore members and 20 lakh charkhas.
The visit of the Prince of Wales (17 November 1921) was met with a nationwide hartal.
Non-Cooperation produced national institutions — Jamia Millia Islamia (Aligarh 1920), Kashi Vidyapith, Gujarat Vidyapith, Bihar Vidyapith.
The programme was to surrender titles and boycott government schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth, plus khadi and Hindu–Muslim unity.
At Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur) on 4 February 1922 a crowd burnt a police station, killing 22 policemen.
The CWC called off the movement by the Bardoli resolution of 12 February 1922.
Gandhi was arrested in March 1922 and sentenced to six years by Judge Broomfield.
The Khilafat issue ended when Mustafa Kemal Atatürk abolished the Caliphate (1924).
The Congress-Khilafat Swaraj Party was founded on 1 January 1923 with C.R. Das as president and Motilal Nehru as secretary.
The 'No-changers' who opposed council entry included Vallabhbhai Patel, Rajendra Prasad, C. Rajagopalachari and M.A. Ansari.
Vithalbhai Patel became the first Indian President (Speaker) of the Central Legislative Assembly in 1925.
The Muddiman Committee (1924) reviewed the working of dyarchy.
The Swaraj Party weakened after C.R. Das died in June 1925.
The All India Trade Union Congress was founded at Bombay in 1920 with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first president.
M.N. Roy founded the Communist Party of India at Tashkent (1920); the Kanpur conference of 1925 organised it in India.
The Congress Socialist Party was formed in 1934 by Acharya Narendra Dev and Jayaprakash Narayan.
The Trade Union Act (1926) recognised trade unions; the Trade Disputes Act (1929) curbed strikes.
The Simon Commission was announced in November 1927 by Secretary of State Lord Birkenhead; all seven members were British MPs, including Clement Attlee.
The Simon Commission landed at Bombay on 3 February 1928 to "Simon Go Back" protests.
Lala Lajpat Rai was lathi-charged at Lahore (30 October 1928) and died on 17 November 1928.
The Simon Commission report (1930) proposed abolishing dyarchy and setting up representative government in the provinces.
The Nehru Report (August 1928), drafted by an All Parties committee chaired by Motilal Nehru, asked for Dominion Status, joint electorates and fundamental rights.
Subhas Bose, Tej Bahadur Sapru and Ali Imam were among the members of the Nehru Report committee.
Jinnah answered the Nehru Report with his Fourteen Points (March 1929).
Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Bose formed the Independence for India League (1928) against the Dominion goal.
Irwin's 'Deepavali Declaration' (31 October 1929) said Dominion Status was the natural goal of India.
At Lahore Nehru hoisted the tricolour on the banks of the Ravi at midnight of 31 December 1929.
The first Independence Day was observed on 26 January 1930 with a public pledge.
Gandhi's Eleven Demands (January 1930) to Irwin included abolition of the salt tax and a 50% cut in land revenue.
Gandhi left Sabarmati on 12 March 1930 with 78 followers and broke the salt law at Dandi on 6 April 1930.
C. Rajagopalachari led a salt march from Trichy to Vedaranyam (Tamil Nadu).
K. Kelappan led the salt march to Payyanur in Malabar.
Sarojini Naidu led the raid on the Dharasana salt works (May 1930); Webb Miller reported the beatings.
Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan ('Frontier Gandhi') led the Khudai Khidmatgars (Red Shirts) in the NWFP.
At Peshawar (Qissa Khwani Bazaar, April 1930) the Garhwal Rifles under Chandra Singh Garhwali refused to fire on the crowd.
Rani Gaidinliu, a Naga leader, joined the movement at 13 and was jailed in 1932; Nehru called her "Rani".
Textile workers in Sholapur set up a parallel administration in May 1930.
Gandhi was arrested on 4–5 May 1930 and held at Yerawada.
The Gandhi–Irwin (Delhi) Pact was signed on 5 March 1931.
The First Round Table Conference (12 November 1930–19 January 1931, London) met without the Congress.
At the Second Round Table Conference (September–December 1931) Gandhi was the sole Congress representative; it failed on the minorities question.
The Third Round Table Conference (November–December 1932) was boycotted by the Congress; Ambedkar and Tej Bahadur Sapru attended all three.
Civil Disobedience resumed in January 1932 under Willingdon and was withdrawn in 1934.
Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award on 16 August 1932, granting separate electorates also to the Depressed Classes.
The Poona Pact (24 September 1932) between Gandhi and Ambedkar replaced separate electorates with 147 reserved seats for the Depressed Classes (71 under the Award).
The 1935 Act proposed an All-India Federation of provinces and princely states, which never came into being.
The 1935 Act abolished dyarchy in the provinces, gave them autonomy and proposed dyarchy at the Centre.
The 1935 Act divided powers into Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists; residuary powers went to the Viceroy.
The 1935 Act set up a Federal Court (1937) at Delhi.
The Reserve Bank of India was set up in 1935.
The 1935 Act made six provinces bicameral — Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam and United Provinces.
The 1935 Act separated Burma from India (1937) and created Sind and Orissa as provinces (1936).
Nehru called the 1935 Act 'a machine with strong brakes but no engine' and 'a charter of slavery'.
The 1935 Act provided for a Federal Public Service Commission and Provincial PSCs, and extended separate electorates to women and labour.
In the 1937 elections the Congress won majorities in five provinces (Madras, UP, CP, Bihar, Orissa) and was the largest party in Bombay.
C. Rajagopalachari became Premier of Madras Presidency (1937).
The Congress ministries resigned in October–November 1939 because Viceroy Linlithgow declared India at war without consulting Indians.
The Muslim League celebrated 22 December 1939 as 'Day of Deliverance' from Congress rule.
Linlithgow's August Offer (8 August 1940) promised Dominion Status after the war, a bigger Executive Council and a War Advisory Council.
The Muslim League's Lahore Resolution (23 March 1940), moved by Fazlul Haq, demanded independent states for Muslim-majority areas.
The name 'Pakistan' was coined by Choudhary Rahmat Ali (1933); Iqbal had proposed a north-western Muslim state at Allahabad (1930).
Individual Satyagraha began on 17 October 1940 with Vinoba Bhave as the first satyagrahi and Jawaharlal Nehru as the second.
The Cripps Mission (March 1942) offered Dominion Status after the war, a constituent assembly and the right of provinces to stay out.
Gandhi called the Cripps offer 'a post-dated cheque' (the phrase 'on a crashing bank' was added by others).
The Working Committee adopted the Quit India idea at Wardha on 14 July 1942; the AICC passed it at Gowalia Tank, Bombay, on 8 August 1942.
In "Operation Zero Hour" on 9 August 1942 Gandhi and the Congress leaders were arrested; Gandhi was held at the Aga Khan Palace, Poona.
Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the Congress flag at Gowalia Tank on 9 August 1942 and became the "heroine of 1942".
Usha Mehta ran the secret Congress Radio from Bombay during Quit India.
Jayaprakash Narayan escaped from Hazaribagh jail (November 1942) to lead the underground; Lohia, Achyut Patwardhan and Sucheta Kripalani also worked underground.
A parallel government was set up at Ballia (UP) in August 1942 under Chittu Pandey.
The Jatiya Sarkar of Tamluk (Midnapore) functioned from December 1942 to September 1944.
The Prati Sarkar of Satara (Y.B. Chavan, Nana Patil) was the longest-lasting parallel government (1943–45).
Gandhi fasted for 21 days in February 1943; Kasturba died at the Aga Khan Palace in February 1944.
The Muslim League, the Communist Party (after the USSR joined the war), the Hindu Mahasabha and the princes kept away from Quit India.
The C.R. (Rajagopalachari) Formula (1944) offered a post-war plebiscite in Muslim-majority areas; Jinnah rejected it.
Gandhi and Jinnah held talks in Bombay in September 1944 on the basis of the C.R. Formula; they failed.
The Desai–Liaquat Pact (January 1945) between Bhulabhai Desai and Liaquat Ali Khan proposed parity in an interim government.
The Wavell Plan led to the Simla Conference (25 June–14 July 1945), which failed over the League's claim to nominate all Muslim members.
The INA trials began at the Red Fort in November 1945 and roused the whole country.
The Royal Indian Navy ratings mutinied in Bombay on 18 February 1946, starting on HMIS Talwar.
Vallabhbhai Patel and Jinnah persuaded the naval ratings to surrender (23 February 1946).
The Cabinet Mission (March 1946) was Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander, sent by Attlee.
The Cabinet Mission Plan (16 May 1946) rejected Pakistan, proposed a weak union and grouped provinces into sections A, B and C.
The League's Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) led to the "Great Calcutta Killings" under Bengal premier H.S. Suhrawardy.
The Interim Government took office on 2 September 1946 with Nehru as Vice-President of the Executive Council; the League joined on 26 October (Liaquat as Finance Member).
The Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946; the League boycotted it.
Attlee announced on 20 February 1947 that Britain would leave India by June 1948.
Mountbatten's 3 June 1947 Plan partitioned India and advanced independence to 15 August 1947.
The Indian Independence Act received royal assent on 18 July 1947 and created two dominions from 15 August 1947.
Sir Cyril Radcliffe chaired the boundary commissions that drew the Punjab and Bengal borders.
Mountbatten was free India's first Governor-General; C. Rajagopalachari was the last (and only Indian) Governor-General; Jinnah became Pakistan's.
The Sapru Committee (1944–45) on the communal deadlock proposed a constituent assembly and minority safeguards.
The Indigo Revolt (1859–60) in Bengal began in Nadia under the Biswas brothers (Digambar and Bishnucharan).
Dinabandhu Mitra's play Neel Darpan (1860) exposed the planters; Rev. James Long was jailed for publishing its English version.
The government appointed an Indigo Commission in 1860.
The Pabna agrarian league (1873–76) of Ishan Chandra Roy and Shambhu Pal fought rent hikes by legal means; the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 followed.
The Deccan Riots (1875) began at Supa in Poona district against Marwari and Gujarati moneylenders; the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act 1879 followed.
The UP Kisan Sabha was founded in 1918 by Gauri Shankar Mishra and Indra Narayan Dwivedi with Madan Mohan Malaviya's support.
Baba Ramchandra, a Fiji-returned labourer, led the Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920), with Jawaharlal Nehru among its organisers.
The Eka (unity) movement (1921–22) in north Awadh was led by Madari Pasi.
The Moplah (Mappila) rebellion of 1921 in Malabar ended in the "Wagon Tragedy", when prisoners suffocated in a closed railway wagon (bound for Podanur).
The Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) under Vallabhbhai Patel resisted a 22% revenue increase; the Maxwell–Broomfield inquiry cut it to 6.03%.
Swami Sahajanand Saraswati formed the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha in 1929.
The All India Kisan Sabha was founded at Lucknow on 11 April 1936 with Swami Sahajanand Saraswati as president and N.G. Ranga as secretary.
The Tebhaga movement (1946–47) of the Bengal Kisan Sabha demanded two-thirds of the crop for sharecroppers (bargadars).
The Telangana armed struggle (1946–51) fought the Nizam's jagirdars, deshmukhs and Razakars and the system of vetti.
The Punnapra–Vayalar revolt (1946) in Travancore was a communist-led rising against the Dewan C.P. Ramaswami Iyer.
The Warli tribal revolt (1945–46) in Thane was led by Godavari Parulekar of the Kisan Sabha.
The Santhal Hul (1855–56) in the Rajmahal hills was led by Sidhu and Kanhu; the Santhal Parganas district was created after it.
The Kol rising (1831–32) in Chotanagpur was led by Buddho Bhagat.
Birsa Munda's Ulgulan (1899–1900) in the Ranchi region ended with his death in jail (June 1900); the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908 followed.
Birsa Munda's birthday, 15 November, is observed as Janjatiya Gaurav Divas.
The Khond uprisings (1837–56) from Odisha into the Srikakulam–Visakhapatnam hills were led by Chakra Bisoi, against the suppression of human sacrifice (meriah) and new taxes.
The Koya revolts of the Godavari agency (1803–1886) were led by chiefs such as Tomma Dora; the 1879–80 Rampa rising and the 1886 revolt of Raja Anantayyar followed.
The Bhil revolts (1817–19) in Khandesh followed famine, distress and Company rule.
The Ramosis of the Western Ghats rose under Chittur Singh (1822) and Umaji Naik after losing Maratha service.
The Khasi rising (1829–33) under Tirot Singh opposed a road linking the Brahmaputra valley with Sylhet.
The Pahariyas of the Rajmahal hills rose in 1778; the British declared their land damni-kol.
The Tana Bhagat movement (1914) of the Oraons was led by Jatra Bhagat.
The Zeliangrong (Heraka) movement in Manipur–Naga hills was led by Jadonang and then Rani Gaidinliu.
The Bastar rebellion (1910) was led by Gunda Dhur.
Amrita Bazar Patrika (1868) was founded by Sisir Kumar Ghosh and Motilal Ghosh; it switched to English overnight (1878) to escape the Vernacular Press Act.
The Hindu (1878, Madras) was started by G. Subramania Iyer and M. Veeraraghavachariar, who also ran Swadesamitran (1882).
The Tribune (1881, Lahore) was founded by Dyal Singh Majithia.
The Bengalee (1862) was later edited by Surendranath Banerjee (from 1879).
Dadabhai Naoroji ran the Gujarati paper Rast Goftar (1851).
Madan Mohan Malaviya founded The Leader (Allahabad, 1909).
Jawaharlal Nehru founded the National Herald (Lucknow, 1938).
The Hindustan Times began at Delhi in 1924 (the source PDF credits K.M. Panikkar, its first editor).
B.R. Ambedkar ran the Marathi fortnightly Bahishkrit Bharat (1927).
Sachindranath Sanyal wrote Bandi Jivan (A Life of Captivity).
The Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act 1908 let magistrates seize presses printing incitement.
The Indian Press Act 1910 revived the harsh provisions of the Vernacular Press Act and demanded securities from presses.
